A multi-objective simulation optimization procedure can be used to find management regimes that best satisfy multiple objectives in multi-ownership landscapes, while accounting for uncertainty and uncoordinated response of landowners.

the optimization of management rules to meet multiple landscape-level objectives in a multi-ownership landscape is challenging, but can be addressed by developing simulation models that forecast trends in landscape pattern in response to management rules implemented by individual landowners, and by combining these models with multi-objective optimization algorithms.

the optimization of management regimes for multiple-objectives under uncoordinated management by multiple land owners is a complex challenge that can be tackled by a multi-objective optimization procedure that combines a genetic algorithm with a simulator that forecasts the effects of management rules on landscape pattern.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we developed a simulation-optimization tool for optimizing the management of landscapes with multiple private landowners, which was applied to a case study in cork oak landscapes.
we have developed a novel multi-objective procedure for the optimization of landscape services, that can be applied in situations where management is not coordinated across private properties.

we developed a multi-objective procedure that can help land managers select management rules that best meet a range of landscape objectives while accounting for uncontrolled and uncertain management by individual landowners, and that can be adapted to different socio-ecological contexts.
The main takeaway from our work is that

it is possible to identify management regimes for multi-owner landscapes that can deliver the desired landscape pattern and services, even in the presence of imperfect compliance with the management rules.
the optimization of landscape services under uncoordinated management by multiple land owners is a feasible problem.

, when dealing with uncoordinated management by multiple landholders, it is possible to find a set of management regimes that, although not necessarily optimal for all landowners, are nevertheless optimal for the landscape as a whole.
